description:
We are 3T Engineers, three computer engineering students at Eskişehir Technical University: 

Sadık Bora Erteni and Deniz Aslan from Türkiye

Kamar Abid from Tunisia 

We love coding, space and turning raw data into something people can explore. This weekend we will take on the challenge of finding places on Earth where crews could rehearse for the Moon and Mars. Using open NASA data, we want to build an interactive way to see where these worlds are alike and where they are not.
summary: What if we could rehearse a Moon base or a Mars landing before ever leaving Earth? Earth Analogs is an interactive 3D website that finds the places on our own planet where astronauts and rovers can do exactly that. Most analog studies begin with a site someone else already chose. We began with the data. Using NASA elevation, thermal and illumination maps, we applied published mission limits to all of Mars and base-site rules to the lunar south pole, and picked our own targets: 5 safe Mars landing zones and 3 ridges for a permanent Moon base. Then we tested our rules against history. Finally, we scored all land on Earth against every site on terrain, rock type, dryness and temperature, and kept three training areas per site: 24 in total. Each one comes with an honest report: where it matches, where it does not, what can be tested there, and what no place on Earth can reproduce, such as low gravity, vacuum and space radiation. Every number was checked by an audit of 167 independent tests.
details:
THE PROBLEM

Before anyone builds a base on the Moon or lands a crew on Mars, every tool, suit and procedure will be rehearsed on Earth. Where that rehearsal happens matters: a test in the wrong kind of place tests the wrong thing. Yet most analog work begins with a familiar field site and asks afterwards what it resembles. And "Mars" is not one place: a dusty plain, a lava field and a river delta need different rehearsals.

OUR ANSWER

Earth Analogs is an interactive 3D website that starts from the destination. Pick a landing site on the Moon or Mars, fly to its closest matches on Earth, and read an honest report on each: what is similar, what is different, what could be tested there, and what Earth can never offer.

We also chose the destinations ourselves. Instead of starting from sites that others have selected, we screened Mars and the lunar south pole with NASA maps and published mission limits, found our own sites, tested our rules on real missions, and only then searched the Earth.

HOW IT WORKS: THREE ACTS

ACT I: WHERE WOULD WE LAND?

Mars. We screened the whole planet with five rules. Four come from mission documents (the Curiosity engineering guide and the Perseverance site selection); the fifth is our own.

  • Low ground (elevation at or below -1 km), so there is enough air for a parachute to brake in.
  • Within 30 degrees of the equator, for warmth and for solar power in winter.
  • Firm ground, not deep dust (thermal inertia of at least 100, and not bright, dusty soil).
  • Gentle slopes (3 degrees or less, measured over kilometres).
  • Low relief (no more than 500 m of height difference across an 18 km area). This is our own rule.

Only 4.5 % of Mars passes all five: 6.45 million km2, a little less than the area of Australia. From the largest safe areas we chose 5 landing zones, each more than 500 km from every past landing: southern Utopia Planitia, northern Elysium Planitia, western Isidis Planitia, the Chryse-Acidalia plains and eastern Meridiani Planum.

The Moon. A permanent base at the south pole needs power, a radio link home, level ground and water ice within reach. We turned these into four rules.

  • Sunlit at least half of the time.
  • Earth visible at least half of the time.
  • Slope of 10 degrees or less.
  • No more than 10 km from a permanently shadowed area of at least 1 km2, where ice can survive.

No mission has published limits for a permanent base, so these thresholds are our own, and the site says so. Three ridges pass every rule. Two lie next to NASA's de Gerlache Rim 2 region, which our screening never used as an input. The third, the Cabeus-Malapert ridge, lies outside NASA's regions.

ACT II: WOULD HISTORY AGREE?

A rule is only worth trusting if it survives a test, so we ran every past landing through ours.

On Mars, 6 of 11 past landings pass every rule, and the failures are the interesting part. Curiosity and Perseverance fail only the low-relief rule: they went to a mountain and a river delta on purpose, with guided landing systems built for that risk. Viking 2, Phoenix and Mars 3 fail the latitude rule: Viking was nuclear powered, and Phoenix flew north to find ice. A landing that fails our rules is not a bad site. It flew a different mission. Every landing whose own published limits we could find passes those limits on our maps.

On the Moon, 4 of the 7 named Artemis III features have passing ground within 25 km. The three robotic landers near the south pole (Chandrayaan-3, IM-1 and IM-2) fail as base sites, as expected for missions designed to last one lunar day.

ACT III: WHERE ON EARTH?

We ranked all land on Earth, on a 0.25 degree grid, against each of the eight sites.

  • Terrain: slopes measured the same way and at the same pixel size on both worlds.
  • Rock type: the unit on the USGS geologic map of Mars against a global rock map of Earth.
  • Dryness: 23 years of NASA rainfall data, plus bare ground.
  • Temperature: the swing between day and night, and cold.
  • For Mars: ground brightness and thin air. For the Moon: a low Sun and frozen ground.

The three best places per site, at least 500 km apart, became its training areas: 24 in all. One button flies you from a site on Mars or the Moon to its training areas on Earth, with real orbital close-ups of both places.

WHY IT MATTERS

  • A shortlist for a specific site. Mission planners and analog-research teams get three ranked training areas for each landing zone or base ridge, with a score for every dimension, not a general answer for "Mars".
  • New places, closer to more people. 21 of our 24 training areas are not on the usual lists of analog sites. The 24 areas span the Sahara, the Arabian Peninsula, the Mongolian Plateau, southern Namibia, Siberia and the Canadian Arctic, among others. Universities and space agencies in those regions may have an analog site within reach that nobody had pointed out to them.
  • A method that can be rerun. If NASA changes its Artemis regions, or a new Mars mission publishes new limits, the same open pipeline produces a new list. Anyone who disagrees with one of our thresholds can change it and see what moves.
  • A way to learn. Students and the public can see why a place was chosen, and why a famous landing site would fail another mission's rules.

WHAT IS NEW

  • We turned the challenge around. We chose the sites from the data first, and used real missions and NASA's Artemis III regions as the exam for our rules, not as the starting point.
  • We treat a failed rule as a story. Each failure explains what that mission was really after.
  • We show weak matches as clearly as strong ones. Mars matches score 77 to 88 out of 100. Moon matches score only 47 to 62, because no cold, dry place on Earth is as steep as a lunar polar ridge, and the reports say so plainly.
  • We audited ourselves in public. The 27 errors we found in our own work are documented, each with its cause and its fix.
  • One continuous 3D scene carries you from the Moon or Mars to Earth, so the comparison is something you see, not only read.

WHY YOU CAN TRUST IT

  • Every rule has a source. Each threshold is traced to a mission document, or clearly labelled as our own choice.
  • The rules were tested on reality: 11 past Mars landings, 7 Artemis III features and 3 lunar landers, as described in Act II.
  • An audit script compares every output with something we did not produce: published landing-site elevations, known geology, weather-station records, the raw data computed a second way, and tests for maps that are shifted, flipped or mirrored. It caught, for example, a Mars dust map being read half a planet away from the elevation map. Final run: 167 checks passed, 0 warnings, 0 failed.
  • It is finished and working. The website is live, loads without a login, works on phones, and has no server or database that could fail. Every figure has a plain-language explanation and a Details panel with formulas and tables.
  • It is reproducible. All input data is public, and the code is open.

HOW IT ANSWERS THE CHALLENGE

The challenge asks for Earth locations that are analogs of permanent Moon-base locations and of Mars. Point by point:

  • "Which characteristics make a strong analogy": every report scores terrain, rock type, dryness, temperature and more, one by one.
  • "Where the analogy breaks down": every report has a section on what differs, and a fixed line on what no place on Earth can reproduce: lunar and Martian gravity, the vacuum, the thin carbon dioxide air of Mars and space radiation.
  • "How the analog helps prepare": every report lists tests that fit the place, and where such tests have been done before.
  • "Don't just rediscover well-known analogs": 21 of 24 training areas are new. Where a match is a known analog region, the report says so.
  • "Think beyond visual similarity": no image comparison is used. Every match is computed from measured terrain, rock, climate and temperature data.
  • "Use multiple datasets together": more than 15 datasets, combined on common grids.

NASA data is the core of every step, not a decoration:

  • Mars screening: MGS MOLA elevation, MGS TES thermal inertia and albedo.
  • Moon screening: LRO LOLA slopes, illumination, Earth visibility and permanent shadow maps.
  • Earth matching: GPM IMERG rainfall, MODIS land surface temperature, vegetation, land cover and albedo.
  • Checks and visuals: NASA landing-site documents, LRO images, THEMIS and LRO WAC mosaics, Blue Marble.

ESA Copernicus elevation data and Sentinel-2 imagery complete the Earth side.

WHAT WE COULD NOT DO

  • Scale: our screening works at about 3.7 km per pixel on Mars and 240 m on the Moon. Real site selection uses metre-scale images and takes years. Our zones are starting points, not certified landing ellipses.
  • Not screened on Mars: rock abundance, metre-scale slopes and winds, because we found no global map we could download and verify.
  • Data limits: the global rock map of Earth is coarse (about 50 km), satellite rainfall reads high in the driest deserts, and a "low Sun" on Earth is never as low as at the lunar pole.

TECH STACK

  • Data pipeline: Python with rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, GeoPandas, earthaccess and pydantic. It screens Mars and the Moon, builds a global Earth grid, ranks the matches, writes the reports and saves everything as small, validated JSON files.
  • Website: React, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS.
  • 3D scene: three.js with three-globe. The Moon, Earth and Mars share one scene, with NASA and USGS textures and live orbital close-ups (THEMIS for Mars, LRO WAC for the Moon, Sentinel-2 for Earth).
  • Hosting: Vercel, as a static site.

GitHub repository: https://github.com/3TEngineers/earth-analogs

Note: The Logo of the team is SI generated.
